title: Clustered cash deposits by Limestone Industrial Supply Inc. across multiple branches
body:
This matter involves Limestone Industrial Supply Inc., a business customer maintaining account 27-44536-1. The case arose from a review of cash transaction activity identified by the automated monitoring system. The relationship manager noted that branch personnel had recently submitted an internal referral after the customer inquired about cash reporting limits at the teller window. A review of account activity was subsequently initiated to determine if the deposit patterns were consistent with attempts to evade regulatory reporting requirements.

The analysis focused on a series of cash deposits made into the customer's account over a ninety-day review period. The aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period was $1,546,407.46. The reviewing analyst observed that these deposits were frequently clustered in amounts between $5,675.36 and $1,087.01. For instance, on a single business day, individual deposits of $8,914.31, $9,640.34, and $9,360.01 were observed. Furthermore, the analysis revealed a pattern of branch rotation, with these deposits often conducted at different Cortex Bank and Trust locations on the same day. Following these deposits, the funds were typically moved out of the account via outbound transfers, the largest of which was for $230,387.93. The combination of customer inquiries regarding reporting thresholds, clustered sub-threshold deposit amounts, and branch rotation on the same day is consistent with the strategic placement of funds to circumvent currency transaction reporting.

The reviewing analyst also considered whether the outbound transfers were indicative of a scenario where funds were induced out of a customer account by deception and moved by wire to a beneficiary the customer never intended to pay. The analysis considered the possibility of business email compromise, particularly concerning the origination of the largest outbound transfer. However, a review of the SWIFT code and correspondent routing associated with the transfers did not reveal anomalies typical of such schemes. Furthermore, the customer did not report any instances of a vendor payment instruction change that would corroborate this alternative explanation.

title: Frequent deposits just below reporting limits across multiple Cortex Bank and Trust locations by Bluewater Ventures Holdings Ltd.
body:
A review of the transaction history for account 48-86195-1, held by Bluewater Ventures Holdings Ltd., was initiated following an automated alert generated by the bank's transaction monitoring system on April 17, 2023. The alert identified a pattern of cash deposits that appeared designed to circumvent regulatory reporting requirements. Over a six-month period, the aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period reached $2,178,207.89. The reviewing analyst noted that a significant portion of this total was composed of deposits clustered between $7,593.00 and $6,395.00. For instance, specific transactions included an individual sub-threshold cash deposit of $9,402.71, a second of $9,709.47, and a third of $9,085.06.

The analysis of these deposits revealed multiple red flags consistent with an attempt to evade Currency Transaction Report (CTR) filing. The deposits were consistently held just below the $10,000 threshold. Furthermore, the customer exhibited a pattern of branch rotation within a single business day, making multiple sub-threshold deposits at different Cortex Bank and Trust locations. Teller reports also indicated that representatives of the customer had asked questions about reporting thresholds. Following the series of deposits, the funds were typically moved out of the account in larger increments, with the largest single outbound transfer during the review period being $265,903.06. Based on these observations, the activity is consistent with a customer breaking cash into sub-threshold increments to defeat currency transaction reporting.

During the investigation, the reviewing analyst also considered whether the activity might represent an exposure to a sanctioned party or jurisdiction that screening either missed or flagged and the business escalated incorrectly. However, a review of the counterparties involved in the outbound transfers did not reveal a sanctioned jurisdiction nexus. While some initial screening alerts were generated on counterparties, these were determined to be a name-match false positive. Additionally, an analysis of the beneficial ownership structure of Bluewater Ventures Holdings Ltd. and its counterparties found no evidence that any sanctioned individual or entity met the fifty percent ownership rule. Therefore, this alternative hypothesis was not adopted.

title: Frequent Same-Day Currency Deposits by Eamon Chanthavong Across Multiple Local Branches
body:

During this time, the customer conducted a significant volume of cash deposits at various branch locations, frequently utilizing multiple branches on the same business day. Branch personnel recorded an interaction during which the customer made specific inquiries regarding the dollar amount at which the bank was obligated to report cash transactions to the government. The analysis focused on the aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period, which totaled $406,110.82. The customer demonstrated a consistent pattern of breaking larger sums of physical currency into smaller increments for deposit, a practice consistent with an attempt to evade the $10,000 currency transaction reporting requirement. Examples of this activity included an individual deposit of $9,250.71, followed closely by deposits of $8,686.96 and $8,361.26, often conducted on consecutive days or the same day at different branches. The funds were subsequently aggregated within the account. The reviewing analyst determined that the customer's inquiries at the teller line, combined with the subsequent pattern of branch rotation and deposit amounts situated just below the regulatory threshold, indicated an intentional effort to defeat currency transaction reporting. No legitimate business purpose was identified for the volume or pattern of cash handling, as the customer’s stated occupation did not align with a cash-intensive enterprise.

The reviewing analyst also considered whether the activity was instead funds induced out of a customer account by deception and moved by wire to a beneficiary the customer never intended to pay. Furthermore, an examination of the SWIFT code and correspondent routing associated with the transfer revealed that the funds were directed to a domestic institution where the customer is a known account holder, rather than an unrelated third-party beneficiary.
